claim: Mice were trained to perform a memory-guided visual discrimination task with stimulus, delay, and response epochs separated by a retractable spout.
source: We trained head-fixed mice to perform a visual discrimination task with a memory-guided response (Figure 1A). In this task, water-restricted mice were presented a 2 s drifting grating stimulus at one of two orientations (0°, 90° from vertical), followed by a variable delay period (0-, 3-, or 6-s), at which point a lick spout was moved rapidly into reach with a linear actuator for 1.5 s (Figure 1B, bottom).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design and task structure used in the study.

claim: Licking on 'go' trials was rewarded with water while licking on 'no-go' trials was punished with quinine.
source: Licking on 'go' trials (horizontal grating drifting toward 0° from vertical) was rewarded with 5–8 μl water (hit), while licking on 'no-go' trials (vertical grating drifting toward 90° from vertical) was punished with 2 μl water containing 5 mM quinine hydrochloride (false alarm; Figure 1B, top; Video 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the reward and punishment contingencies of the task.

claim: After extensive training, mice reliably exhibited strong differences in licking between go and no-go trials for all delay period durations.
source: After extensive training (117 ± 11 behavioral sessions, 299 ± 25 trials per session; mean ± s.e.m.), mice reliably exhibited strong differences in licking between go and no-go trials (Figure 1C, top) for all delay period durations.
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral data showing differential licking responses, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Mice performance decreased slightly with longer delays but was well above chance for all delay durations.
source: Performance decreased slightly with longer delays, but was well above chance for all delay durations (0 s Delay, p<10−9; 3 s Delay, p<10−9; 6 s Delay, p<10−9; t-test, n = 8 mice across 80 sessions).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of behavioral performance across different delay conditions.

claim: Video analysis showed that mice did not exhibit postural changes or increased movement during the delay period.
source: Video analysis showed that mice did not exhibit postural changes or increased movement during the delay period (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; see Video 1 for representative mouse performance).
evidence: The manuscript reports video analysis results with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: A total of 9,150 active neurons were imaged in regions V1, PPC, and fMC.
source: A total of 9,150 active neurons were imaged in regions V1 (n = 2,695 neurons), PPC (n = 3,552), and fMC (n = 2,903), of which 3,049 (33.3%) exhibited trial-locked responses significantly different from baseline (see Materials and methods for inclusion criteria; Figure 1G).
evidence: The manuscript reports the total number of neurons recorded across different brain regions.

claim: 33.3% of active neurons exhibited trial-locked responses significantly different from baseline.
source: A total of 9,150 active neurons were imaged in regions V1 (n = 2,695 neurons), PPC (n = 3,552), and fMC (n = 2,903), of which 3,049 (33.3%) exhibited trial-locked responses significantly different from baseline (see Materials and methods for inclusion criteria; Figure 1G).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of neurons with significant task-related responses.

claim: The majority (63%) of V1 neurons with increased task-evoked activity exhibited robust responses during the stimulus epoch but not during other epochs.
source: The majority (63%, Figure 3, see below for description of classification procedure) of V1 neurons with increased task-evoked activity exhibited robust and reliable responses during the stimulus epoch but not during other epochs of the task, with similar responses across 0, 3, and 6 s delays (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion and characteristics of V1 neurons responding during the stimulus epoch.

claim: 37% of V1 neurons exhibited activity during other task epochs, particularly during the response epoch.
source: However, there was also a sizable fraction (37%) of neurons that exhibited activity during the other task epochs, particularly during the response epoch (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of V1 neurons active during non-stimulus epochs.

claim: 53% of responsive V1 neurons were suppressed throughout the stimulus and delay periods in a delay duration-dependent fashion.
source: Interestingly, there was an additional fraction (53% of responsive neurons) of neurons that were suppressed throughout the stimulus and delay periods in a delay duration-dependent fashion (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of V1 neurons showing suppressed activity.

claim: Neurons exhibiting delay-dependent suppression have not been previously described in V1 despite their prevalence in this sample.
source: To our knowledge, neurons exhibiting delay-dependent suppression have not been previously described in V1 despite their prevalence in our sample.
evidence: The manuscript makes a claim about the novelty of the finding relative to existing literature.

claim: Single-unit electrophysiological recordings in V1 during behavior found a sizable fraction of neurons with suppressed responses (10/21 single units).
source: To ensure that the suppressed activity pattern was not an artifact of the calcium imaging technique, we carried out single-unit electrophysiological recordings in two mice using silicon probes in V1 during behavior and found a sizable fraction of neurons with suppressed responses during behavior (10/21 single units; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological validation of the suppressed neuron finding.

claim: 48% of enhanced PPC neurons exhibited activity during both stimulus and response epochs.
source: Neurons in PPC were even more heterogeneous, with a large number (48% of enhanced neurons) of neurons exhibiting activity during both stimulus and response epochs (Figure 2E,F)
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of PPC neurons active during multiple task epochs.

claim: 11% of enhanced PPC neurons exhibited delay-dependent enhanced activity.
source: as well as some neurons (11% of enhanced neurons) exhibiting delay-dependent enhanced activity (Figure 2G), as has previously been observed in primate experiments in delayed-response tasks (Chafee and Goldman-Rakic, 1998; Constantinidis and Steinmetz, 1996).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of PPC neurons with delay-period activity and cites prior work.

claim: Suppressed delay-dependent activity in PPC was much less prevalent compared to V1 (9% vs. 53%).
source: Finally, we again saw neurons that exhibited suppressed delay-dependent activity during the task (Figure 2H), though they were much less prevalent compared to V1 (9% vs. 53% for PPC and V1, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript compares the prevalence of suppressed neurons between brain regions.

claim: 47% of enhanced fMC neurons responded solely during the response epoch.
source: As expected in motor regions, a plurality (47% of enhanced neurons) of neurons responded solely during the response epoch (Figure 2I).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of fMC neurons responding during the response epoch.

claim: 33% of enhanced fMC neurons responded during both the response epoch and in a sustained manner throughout the delay period.
source: However, a substantial fraction (33% of enhanced neurons) of neurons responded not only during the response epoch, but also in a sustained manner throughout the delay period (Figure 2J)
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of fMC neurons with sustained delay-period activity.

claim: The sustained activity in fMC cannot be attributed to the slow decay of the GCaMP6 indicator because the duration of sustained activity varies parametrically with delay period duration.
source: Note that the sustained activity cannot be attributed to the slow decay of the GCaMP6 indicator after the initial stimulus response, as the duration of the sustained activity varies parametrically with the duration of the delay period.
evidence: The manuscript provides reasoning to rule out an alternative explanation for the observed sustained activity.

claim: 39% of responsive fMC neurons exhibited suppressed delay-dependent activity.
source: Finally, we again observed a subset (39% of responsive neurons) of neurons with suppressed delay-dependent activity in fMC (Figure 2L).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of fMC neurons with suppressed activity.

claim: Hierarchical clustering revealed six distinct response types: four enhanced and two suppressed.
source: Hierarchical clustering revealed six distinct response types, four of them exhibiting enhanced activity and two exhibiting suppressed activity (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of clustering analysis on neural responses.

claim: The four enhanced response classes are: stimulus-driven (Stim only), response-driven (Resp only), stimulus- and response-driven (Stim+Resp), and delay-driven (Delay).
source: To reveal the archetypical response of each group, we averaged the normalized responses of all neurons within each cluster, revealing four enhanced response classes: stimulus-driven (Stim only), response-driven (Resp only), stimulus- and response-driven (Stim+Resp), and delay-driven (Delay), as well as two suppressed response classes: delay-sensitive stimulus-driven (Supp. Delay early) and delay-sensitive response-driven (Supp. Delay late; Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the classification of neural response types based on clustering.

claim: The two suppressed response classes are: delay-sensitive stimulus-driven (Supp. Delay early) and delay-sensitive response-driven (Supp. Delay late).
source: To reveal the archetypical response of each group, we averaged the normalized responses of all neurons within each cluster, revealing four enhanced response classes: stimulus-driven (Stim only), response-driven (Resp only), stimulus- and response-driven (Stim+Resp), and delay-driven (Delay), as well as two suppressed response classes: delay-sensitive stimulus-driven (Supp. Delay early) and delay-sensitive response-driven (Supp. Delay late; Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the classification of suppressed neural response types.

claim: There were clear differences in both enhanced and suppressed response types between regions.
source: There were clear differences in both enhanced and suppressed response types between regions, such as V1 containing a large number of 'Stim only' and 'Supp. Delay early' neurons, while fMC had greater numbers of 'Delay', 'Resp only', and 'Supp. Delay late' neurons (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript reports regional differences in the distribution of response types.

claim: All three regions contained a fraction of almost all response types, showing surprising heterogeneity.
source: However, there was a surprising amount of heterogeneity as well, with all three regions containing a fraction of almost all response types.
evidence: The manuscript notes the heterogeneity of response types across regions.

claim: 32.0% of significantly responding neurons exhibited suppressed rather than enhanced responses during task performance.
source: We next investigated what role neurons exhibiting suppressed activity (975/3049 neurons, 32.0%; Figure 2D,H,L) play in encoding task-relevant information.
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of neurons with suppressed activity.

claim: The vast majority of enhanced neurons showed a strong preference for a particular trial type with little or no response to the non-preferred trial type.
source: The vast majority of enhanced neurons showed a strong preference for a particular trial type (hit vs. correct reject, only correct trials included in analysis), with little or no response to the non-preferred trial type (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript describes the selectivity characteristics of enhanced neurons.

claim: The majority of suppressed neurons showed very similar responses to both trial types, with little difference between 'preferred' and 'non-preferred' trial types.
source: However, the majority of suppressed neurons showed very similar responses to both trial types, with little difference between 'preferred' and 'non-preferred' trial types (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the lack of selectivity in suppressed neurons.

claim: Enhanced neurons were significantly more selective than suppressed neurons in all three regions (V1: p<10–9; PPC: p<10–9; fMC: p<10–9).
source: We used a selectivity index ranging from 0 (responds equally to preferred and non-preferred stimuli) to 1 (only responds to preferred stimuli) to quantify the selectivity of each neuron (see Materials and methods), revealing that enhanced neurons were significantly more selective than suppressed neurons in all three regions (Figure 4C; V1: Enh. median SI = 0.67, Supp. median SI = 0.16, p<10–9; PPC: Enh. median SI = 0.91, Supp. median SI = 0.31, p<10–9; fMC: Enh. median SI = 0.99, Supp. median SI = 0.53, p<10–9; Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of selectivity between enhanced and suppressed neurons.

claim: The latencies of suppressed responses were slow (>400 ms) and uncorrelated to the enhanced population latency in the cortical region.
source: We estimated the response latency of the suppressed neurons, and found that the latencies were slow (>400 ms) and uncorrelated to the enhanced population latency in the cortical region (Figure 4D).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of response latencies for suppressed neurons.

claim: Suppressed neurons exhibited suppression throughout the delay period in a duration-dependent manner, even when this pattern was not present in enhanced neurons of the same region.
source: We also found that suppressed neurons exhibited a suppression throughout the delay period (in a duration-dependent manner; Figure 2D,H,L), even when this pattern was not present in the enhanced neurons of the same region (Figure 4E).
evidence: The manuscript reports the temporal characteristics of suppressed neuron activity.

claim: The suppressed responses are not simply reflecting inhibition from local excitatory responses, but rather are the result of more complex dynamics, possibly low-latency, delay-dependent inputs from distal regions.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that the suppressed responses are not simply reflecting inhibition from local excitatory responses, but rather are the result of more complex dynamics; possibly low-latency, delay-dependent inputs from distal regions.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the suppressed neuron findings.

claim: V1 neurons preferred go and no-go trials in roughly equal numbers.
source: While V1 neurons preferred go and no-go trials in roughly equal numbers, we found that PPC and fMC neurons were highly biased toward the go trials (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the distribution of trial preferences in V1.

claim: PPC and fMC neurons were highly biased toward go trials.
source: While V1 neurons preferred go and no-go trials in roughly equal numbers, we found that PPC and fMC neurons were highly biased toward the go trials (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the bias in trial preferences for PPC and fMC neurons.

claim: V1 neurons were predominantly active during the stimulus epoch.
source: Specifically, V1 neurons were predominantly active during the stimulus epoch, while PPC and fMC exhibited more heterogeneous responses spanning stimulus, delay, and response epochs.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal characteristics of V1 population activity.

claim: PPC and fMC exhibited more heterogeneous responses spanning stimulus, delay, and response epochs.
source: Specifically, V1 neurons were predominantly active during the stimulus epoch, while PPC and fMC exhibited more heterogeneous responses spanning stimulus, delay, and response epochs.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal characteristics of PPC and fMC population activity.

claim: Sustained delay-period activity was most prevalent in fMC, both in single-unit and population activity.
source: Although sustained delay-period activity could be observed across all cortical regions, it was most prevalent in fMC, both in single-unit (Figure 3C) and population (Figure 5C) activity.
evidence: The manuscript reports the prevalence of sustained activity across regions.

claim: The first mode of the latency distribution increased from V1 to PPC to fMC for all delay durations (V1: 89 ± 10 ms, PPC: 244 ± 15 ms, fMC: 827 ± 177 ms).
source: Finally, there were considerable differences in latency to significant response, with the first mode of the latency distribution increasing from V1 to PPC to fMC for all delay durations (V1: 89 ± 10 ms, PPC: 244 ± 15 ms, fMC: 827 ± 177 ms, mean across delays; regions all significantly different, V1 x PPC: p<10−9, V1 x fMC: p<10−9, PPC x fMC: p<10−9, Wilcoxon rank-sum test; Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of response latencies across regions.

claim: Neuronal responses in PPC and fMC exhibit more similarity than V1 for trial types with the same motor response.
source: Neuronal responses in PPC and fMC appear to exhibit more similarity than V1 for trial types with the same motor response (Figure 6A, middle and right panels corresponding to hit vs. false alarm trials; Pearson correlation between hit and false alarm trials, V1: 0.23 ± 0.03, PPC: 0.47 ± 0.01, fMC: 0.46 ± 0.02).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis of neural responses for trials with the same motor response.

claim: In V1, stimulus identity could be decoded with perfect accuracy given a sufficient number of neurons.
source: In V1, stimulus identity could be decoded with perfect accuracy given a sufficient number of neurons (Figure 6B, left), while behavioral choice was only weakly encoded (Figure 6C, left).
evidence: The manuscript reports decoding analysis results for V1.

claim: In V1, behavioral choice was only weakly encoded.
source: In V1, stimulus identity could be decoded with perfect accuracy given a sufficient number of neurons (Figure 6B, left), while behavioral choice was only weakly encoded (Figure 6C, left).
evidence: The manuscript reports decoding analysis results for behavioral choice in V1.

claim: In PPC, both stimulus identity and behavioral choice could be decoded with moderate success.
source: In PPC, both stimulus identity and behavioral choice could be decoded with moderate success (Figure 6B,C, middle), although the dynamics were noticeably different.
evidence: The manuscript reports decoding analysis results for PPC.

claim: In PPC, stimulus identity was predominantly encoded early in the trial.
source: Specifically, while the stimulus identity was predominantly encoded early in the trial (statistically significant from 0.6–3.4 s and 7.2–10.0 s), the behavioral choice encoding slightly lagged the stimulus identity encoding, and remained high throughout the trial, peaking during the early part of the licking response (statistically significant from 1.4–10.0 s; Figure 6D, middle).
evidence: The manuscript reports the temporal dynamics of stimulus encoding in PPC.

claim: In PPC, behavioral choice encoding slightly lagged stimulus identity encoding and remained high throughout the trial, peaking during the early part of the licking response.
source: Specifically, while the stimulus identity was predominantly encoded early in the trial (statistically significant from 0.6–3.4 s and 7.2–10.0 s), the behavioral choice encoding slightly lagged the stimulus identity encoding, and remained high throughout the trial, peaking during the early part of the licking response (statistically significant from 1.4–10.0 s; Figure 6D, middle).
evidence: The manuscript reports the temporal dynamics of choice encoding in PPC.

claim: The stimulus encoding is much weaker in PPC than in V1, likely due to the large number of neurons that jointly-encode stimulus and choice information.
source: Note that the stimulus encoding is much weaker in PPC than in V1, likely due to the large number of neurons that jointly-encode stimulus and choice information (Park et al., 2014; Raposo et al., 2014; Pho et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the weaker stimulus encoding in PPC with citations to supporting literature.

claim: In fMC, stimulus identity could not be decoded above chance for the majority of the trial.
source: Finally, in fMC the stimulus identity could not be decoded above chance for the majority of the trial (Figure 6B, right), while the behavioral choice could be decoded with greater accuracy in fMC than in other regions (Figure 6C, right).
evidence: The manuscript reports decoding analysis results for stimulus identity in fMC.

claim: In fMC, behavioral choice could be decoded with greater accuracy than in other regions.
source: Finally, in fMC the stimulus identity could not be decoded above chance for the majority of the trial (Figure 6B, right), while the behavioral choice could be decoded with greater accuracy in fMC than in other regions (Figure 6C, right).
evidence: The manuscript reports decoding analysis results for behavioral choice in fMC.

claim: In fMC, stimulus identity decoding was only above chance during the response epoch.
source: Thus, while stimulus identity decoding was only above chance during the response epoch (statistically significant from 8.8–9.4 s, see caveat on stimulus identity encoding during response epoch above), the behavioral choice could be decoded throughout the delay and response epochs (statistically significant from 3.0–10.0 s; Figure 6D, right).
evidence: The manuscript reports the temporal dynamics of stimulus encoding in fMC.

claim: In fMC, behavioral choice could be decoded throughout the delay and response epochs.
source: Thus, while stimulus identity decoding was only above chance during the response epoch (statistically significant from 8.8–9.4 s, see caveat on stimulus identity encoding during response epoch above), the behavioral choice could be decoded throughout the delay and response epochs (statistically significant from 3.0–10.0 s; Figure 6D, right).
evidence: The manuscript reports the temporal dynamics of choice encoding in fMC.

claim: V1 principally encodes the stimulus identity.
source: By measuring the difference in 'hit' and 'correct reject' trajectories along the 'stimulus' and 'choice' axes, we found once again that V1 principally encodes the stimulus identity (Figure 7A,D), PPC encodes a mixture of stimulus identity and behavioral choice (Figure 7B,E), and fMC predominantly encodes the behavioral choice throughout the stimulus, delay, and response epochs (Figure 7C,F).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from targeted dimensionality reduction analysis for V1.

claim: PPC encodes a mixture of stimulus identity and behavioral choice.
source: By measuring the difference in 'hit' and 'correct reject' trajectories along the 'stimulus' and 'choice' axes, we found once again that V1 principally encodes the stimulus identity (Figure 7A,D), PPC encodes a mixture of stimulus identity and behavioral choice (Figure 7B,E), and fMC predominantly encodes the behavioral choice throughout the stimulus, delay, and response epochs (Figure 7C,F).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from targeted dimensionality reduction analysis for PPC.

claim: fMC predominantly encodes the behavioral choice throughout the stimulus, delay, and response epochs.
source: By measuring the difference in 'hit' and 'correct reject' trajectories along the 'stimulus' and 'choice' axes, we found once again that V1 principally encodes the stimulus identity (Figure 7A,D), PPC encodes a mixture of stimulus identity and behavioral choice (Figure 7B,E), and fMC predominantly encodes the behavioral choice throughout the stimulus, delay, and response epochs (Figure 7C,F).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from targeted dimensionality reduction analysis for fMC.

claim: Laser stimulation (2 s continuous pulses, 6.5 mW mm−2) completely eliminated spikes during the laser stimulation period in all recorded regular-spiking neurons in V1.
source: We found that laser stimulation (2 s continuous pulses, 6.5 mW mm−2) potently inhibited the activity of regular spiking neurons (see example L5 neuron, Figure 8B), completely eliminating spikes during the laser stimulation period in all recorded neurons, even during presentation of a drifting grating stimulus of the preferred orientation (grating presented from 1 s before laser stimulation to 1 s after laser stimulation; Figure 8B, inset, n = 2 mice).
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological validation of optogenetic inhibition efficacy.

claim: After light exposure, VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice showed dramatically reduced expression of c-Fos throughout all layers of the cortex underlying the cranial window.
source: We found that after light exposure, VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice (but not wild-type controls) showed dramatically reduced expression of c-Fos throughout all layers of the cortex underlying our cranial window (Figure 8D,E, n = 3 mice).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunohistochemical characterization of the spatial extent of photoinhibition.

claim: The suppression of c-Fos was confined to within 500 μm laterally from the edge of the window and did not spread past the white matter into subcortical regions.
source: The suppression was confined to within 500 μm laterally from the edge of the window, and did not spread past the white matter into subcortical regions.
evidence: The manuscript reports the spatial extent of photoinhibition based on c-Fos expression.

claim: Bilateral inactivation of V1 during the stimulus epoch impaired performance of VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice (p=0.002) but not wild-type controls (p=0.27).
source: Using a simplified version of the task without a delay period, we confirmed that bilateral inactivation of V1 during the stimulus epoch impaired performance of VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice (p=0.002), but not wild-type controls exposed to the same light stimulation (Δd' = +0.14, p=0.27; Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral effects of V1 photoinhibition with statistical tests.

claim: Inactivation of V1 for 2 s prior to stimulus onset had no effect on performance (Δd' = −0.15, p=0.51).
source: To ensure that inactivation did not have long-lasting effects on the inactivated cortical regions, we inactivated region V1 for 2 s prior to the stimulus onset, and found no effect on performance (Δd' = −0.15, p=0.51); Figure 8—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: The manuscript reports control experiment results showing no lasting effects of photoinhibition.

claim: Photoinhibition of all three regions (V1, PPC, fMC) was capable of disrupting the performance of the task, causing performance to drop to chance levels.
source: Photoinhibition of all three regions was capable of disrupting the performance of the task, causing performance to drop to chance levels. However, the specific task epochs during which laser stimulation disrupted behavior differed for each brain region (Figure 9C).
evidence: The manuscript reports the behavioral effects of photoinhibition across all three regions.

claim: The specific task epochs during which laser stimulation disrupted behavior differed for each brain region.
source: Photoinhibition of all three regions was capable of disrupting the performance of the task, causing performance to drop to chance levels. However, the specific task epochs during which laser stimulation disrupted behavior differed for each brain region (Figure 9C).
evidence: The manuscript reports epoch-specific effects of photoinhibition.

claim: V1 was necessary during the stimulus epoch (d'OFF = 1.51 ± 0.11, d'ON: 0.21 ± 0.11, p<10−3).
source: As expected, V1 (Figure 9C,D, top row) was necessary during the stimulus epoch, with laser stimulation dramatically reducing the animal's ability to perform the task (stimulus: d'OFF = 1.51 ± 0.11, d'ON: 0.21 ± 0.11, p<10−3).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of V1 photoinhibition effects during the stimulus epoch.

claim: Inactivation of V1 during the delay or response epochs had no effect (delay: Δd' = 0.47, p=0.41, response: Δd' = 0.23, p=1.0).
source: However, inactivation of V1 during the delay or response epochs had no effect (delay: Δd' = 0.47, p=0.41, response: Δd' = 0.23, p=1.0).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis showing no effect of V1 photoinhibition during delay or response epochs.

claim: PPC was necessary during the stimulus epoch (d'OFF = 1.81 ± 0.16, d'ON: 0.27 ± 0.12, p<10−3).
source: Activity in PPC (Figure 9C,D; middle row) was also necessary during the stimulus epoch (stimulus: d'OFF = 1.81 ± 0.16, d'ON: 0.27 ± 0.12, p<10−3).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of PPC photoinhibition effects during the stimulus epoch.

claim: Inactivation of PPC during the delay and response periods had no effect on behavior (delay: Δd' = 0.03, p=1.0, response: Δd' = 0.24, p=0.79).
source: However, despite the high level of activity in many PPC neurons during the delay and response periods (Figure 5C; Figure 3—figure supplement 2), inactivation of PPC during these periods had no effect on behavior (delay: Δd' = 0.03, p=1.0, response: Δd' = 0.24, p=0.79).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis showing no effect of PPC photoinhibition during delay or response epochs.

claim: Suppression of fMC during any of the three trial epochs completely abolished performance in the task (stimulus: p<10−4; delay: p<10−4; response: p<10−3).
source: By contrast, suppression of fMC (Figure 9C and D; bottom row) during any of the three trial epochs completely abolished performance in the task (stimulus: d'OFF = 1.37 ± 0.10, d'ON: −0.05 ± 0.13, p<10−4; delay: d'OFF = 1.60 ± 0.10, d'ON: 0.32 ± 0.23, p<10−4; response: d'OFF = 1.60 ± 0.17, d'ON: -0.06 ± 0.05, p<10−3; paired t-test with Bonferroni correction used for all behavioral statistical tests).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of fMC photoinhibition effects across all task epochs.

claim: Stimulus period photoinhibition continues to disrupt behavioral performance for all three regions in a task with shortened stimulus duration of 250 ms.
source: To test this possibility, we trained mice on a similar task with a shortened stimulus duration of 250 ms (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A; performance declined to chance levels with shorter stimulus durations, data not shown). Stimulus period photoinhibition continues to disrupt behavioral performance for all three regions (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B), similar to the longer duration stimulus epochs (Figure 9C).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from a control experiment with shorter stimulus duration.

claim: All three regions (V1, PPC, fMC) are necessary during the stimulus epoch of the task.
source: Our results thus show that all three regions are necessary during the stimulus epoch of the task.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the photoinhibition results across regions.

claim: Only fMC was necessary during the delay and response epochs of the task.
source: Surprisingly, although there was robust task-related activity in PPC during the delay and response epochs, photoinhibition of PPC during these epochs had no impact on the performance of the memory-guided task. Only fMC was necessary during the delay and response epochs of the task, showing that fMC can act independently of V1 and PPC once the stimulus epoch processing is complete.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the epoch-specific necessity of different brain regions.

claim: fMC can act independently of V1 and PPC once the stimulus epoch processing is complete.
source: Only fMC was necessary during the delay and response epochs of the task, showing that fMC can act independently of V1 and PPC once the stimulus epoch processing is complete.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the photoinhibition results.

claim: Despite differences in single-unit activity between regions, the responses within a region were surprisingly heterogeneous, with a representation of all classified response types in all regions.
source: First, large-scale 2-photon calcium imaging revealed that despite differences in single-unit activity between regions, the responses within a region were surprisingly heterogeneous, with a representation of all classified response types in all regions (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes a key finding about heterogeneity of neural responses.

claim: In V1, many neurons were active during the response epoch in addition to the expected neurons active during the stimulus period.
source: For example, in V1 we observed many neurons that were active during the response epoch in addition to the expected neurons active during the stimulus period, and vice versa in the frontal motor cortices.
evidence: The manuscript describes unexpected findings about V1 neural activity.

claim: This study shows, for the first time in mice, that a fraction of neurons (mostly in PPC and fMC) exhibit sustained activity that varies parametrically with delay duration.
source: This study also shows, for the first time in mice, that a fraction of neurons (mostly in PPC and fMC) exhibit sustained activity that varies parametrically with delay duration, in line with earlier work from non-human primates (Fuster and Alexander, 1971; Kojima and Goldman-Rakic, 1982; Funahashi et al., 1989).
evidence: The manuscript claims novelty of the finding in mice and cites prior primate work.

claim: V1 exhibited a moderate bias toward Hit trials (65.3% target-preferring).
source: In particular, while V1 exhibited a moderate bias toward Hit trials (65.3% target-preferring), PPC and fMC exhibited much stronger biases toward Hit trials (95.5% and 97.2% target-selective, respectively), although there was a small fraction of neurons that showed robust responses selective for CR trials (Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of neurons preferring different trial types in V1.

claim: PPC and fMC exhibited much stronger biases toward Hit trials (95.5% and 97.2% target-selective, respectively).
source: In particular, while V1 exhibited a moderate bias toward Hit trials (65.3% target-preferring), PPC and fMC exhibited much stronger biases toward Hit trials (95.5% and 97.2% target-selective, respectively), although there was a small fraction of neurons that showed robust responses selective for CR trials (Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: The manuscript reports the proportion of neurons preferring different trial types in PPC and fMC.

claim: Using volumetric calcium imaging to sample large populations of neurons, evidence was found for steady-state representation of motor choice in this task.
source: Using volumetric calcium imaging to sample large populations of neurons, we found evidence in our task for steady-state representation of motor choice, with the vast majority of delay-sensitive neurons becoming active early in the trial and exhibiting persistent or ramping activity throughout the delay period (Figure 2G,J,K; Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings about the mode of neural activity during delay periods.

claim: The nature of the mnemonic information in the behavioral task has a strong bearing on the mode of activity observed (steady-state vs. sequential).
source: We suspect that the nature of the mnemonic information in the behavioral task has a strong bearing on the mode of activity observed.
evidence: The manuscript provides speculation about factors influencing neural activity patterns.

claim: In tasks where neurons exhibit steady-state activity, the encoded motor plan is held constant throughout the delay period.
source: In tasks where neurons exhibit steady-state activity, such as our study and others (Fuster and Alexander, 1971; Kojima and Goldman-Rakic, 1982; Funahashi et al., 1989; Shadlen and Newsome, 2001), the encoded motor plan is held constant throughout the delay period (e.g., lick when the spout comes forward; make a saccade to a fixed location).
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of steady-state activity with citations to supporting literature.

claim: In tasks where neurons exhibit sequential activity, the encoded motor plan may vary as a function of the trial as the animal navigates through real or virtual space.
source: In contrast, in tasks where neurons exhibit sequential activity (Baeg et al., 2003; Fujisawa et al., 2008; Harvey et al., 2012) the encoded motor plan may vary as a function of the trial as the animal navigates through real or virtual space.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of sequential activity with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Suppressed neurons were generally much less selective than enhanced neurons, particularly in V1 and PPC.
source: A second contribution is the finding that a sizable fraction of the significantly responding neurons (32.0% of all significantly-responding neurons) exhibited suppressed rather than enhanced responses during task performance (Figure 2, Figure 3). However, these neurons were generally much less selective than enhanced neurons (particularly in V1 and PPC), and as a result appear to play little role in encoding task-relevant variables (Figure 4).

claim: The fMC predominantly encodes behavioral choice, beginning early in the trial and lasting throughout the delay period until after the motor response is made.
source: The fMC predominantly encodes behavioral choice, beginning early in the trial and lasting throughout the delay period until after the motor response is made, in accord with choice-related activity observed in premotor regions in earlier rodent (Erlich et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2013, Li et al., 2015) and non-human primate studies (Hernandez et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript describes encoding characteristics of fMC and cites supporting literature.

claim: PPC is necessary for performance during the stimulus epoch of the task.
source: Fourth, we find that PPC is necessary for performance during the stimulus epoch of the task (Figure 9), in contrast to several recent pharmacological and optogenetic perturbation studies in rodents (Guo et al., 2013; Erlich et al., 2015), which found that inactivation of PPC had no effect on behavioral performance in sensorimotor decision tasks.
evidence: The manuscript reports findings about PPC necessity and contrasts with prior studies.

claim: PPC may play a greater role for some sensory modalities than others during sensorimotor decision tasks, perhaps due to differences in anatomy.
source: One possibility is that PPC plays a greater role for some sensory modalities than others during sensorimotor decision tasks, perhaps due to differences in anatomy (e.g., S1 directly projects to motor regions while V1 input reaches motor cortex only indirectly, with PPC as the principal cortical intermediary; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript provides speculation about factors influencing PPC's role with citation to anatomical data.

source: Indeed, a recent study found that pharmacological inhibition of PPC somewhat impaired performance of a rate discrimination task for visual stimuli, but did not affect performance when auditory stimuli were used (Raposo et al., 2014).

claim: PPC may play a greater role for sensorimotor tasks in which higher-level features must be mapped to motor actions, in contrast to tasks involving detection of simple stimuli.
source: Another intriguing possibility is that PPC plays a greater role for sensorimotor tasks in which higher-level features (e.g., orientation) must be mapped to motor actions; in contrast to tasks involving detection of simple stimuli, which may be mediated by subcortical or direct sensory cortex to motor cortex projections.
evidence: The manuscript provides speculation about task-dependent roles of PPC.
